title: Choroidal Nevus vs. Melanoma: Clinical Masterclass
summary: Differentiating a benign choroidal nevus from a life-threatening uveal melanoma is a critical skill for the ophthalmologist. This poster explores the epidemiology, multimodal imaging features, and the 'TFSOM-UHHD' risk assessment used to guide management.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Choroidal nevus is a common, benign intraocular melanocytic tumor (prevalence 5-10%). Uveal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, arising from melanocytes within the uveal tract (choroid 85%, ciliary body 10%, iris 5%). Proper identification is vital to prevent systemic metastasis, primarily to the liver.

content.mnemonic: To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Using Helpful Hints Daily
content.explanation: T: Thickness >2mm; F: Fluid (subretinal); S: Symptoms (flashes/floaters/vision loss); O: Orange pigment (lipofuscin); M: Margin touching optic disc (<3mm); U: Ultrasonographic Hollowness; H: Halo Absence; H: Drusen Absence (Drusen suggest chronicity/benignity).

sections.title: Etiology & Genetics
content: GNAQ/GNA11 Mutations: Found in 85% of both nevi and melanomas (early event).
BAP1 Mutation: Associated with high metastatic risk (Monosomy 3).
SF3B1/EIF1AX: Associated with intermediate/low metastatic risk.
Risk Factors: Fair skin, light iris color, ocular melanocytosis (Nevus of Ota), BAP1-TPDS.

sections.title: Multimodal Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy & Indirect Ophthalmoscopy (Identify lesion location/color).
Step 2: Fundus Photography & Autofluorescence (FAF) to detect orange pigment.
Step 3: Enhanced Depth Imaging (EDI-OCT) to measure thickness and detect subretinal fluid/shaggy photoreceptors.
Step 4: B-scan/A-scan Ultrasonography (Assess reflectivity and dimensions).
Step 5: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) to rule out CNVM or confirm 'double circulation'.
Step 6: Fine Needle Aspiration Biopsy (FNAB) for prognostic GEP (Gene Expression Profiling) if treatment is planned.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Suspicious Nevus: Observation every 3-6 months with serial imaging.
Small Melanoma: Plaque brachytherapy (I-125) or Thermotherapy (TTT) or continued observation if dormant.
Medium Melanoma: Plaque brachytherapy (COMS showed no survival difference vs Enucleation).
Large Melanoma: Enucleation is standard; Brachytherapy if feasible.
Systemic Monitoring: Semi-annual Liver USG, MRI, or CT for metastatic surveillance.

sections.title: Emergency 'Red Flags'
content: Documented growth on serial photography
Presence of sentinel vessels (episcleral congestion)
Extrascleral extension on B-scan
Ciliary body involvement (worse prognosis)
Diffuse 'flat' growth pattern

sections.title: Surgical Techniques: Plaque Brachytherapy
content: Isotopes: Iodine-125 (common), Ruthenium-106, Palladium-103.
Procedure: Peritomy, muscle isolation/tagging, localization with transillumination.
Dose: Usually 85 Gy to the tumor apex.
Plaque stays in place for 4-7 days depending on activity level.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (High Yield)
content: Drusen are your friend; they indicate the lesion has likely been there for years.
Lipofuscin (orange pigment) is the 'hottest' indicator of malignancy.
If a lesion is <2mm but has 3+ risk factors, treat it as a melanoma.
Always check the other eye; uveal melanoma is almost always unilateral.

sections.title: Landmark Study: COMS Trial
sections.content: The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) established that: 1) There is no survival difference between enucleation and Iodine-125 brachytherapy for medium-sized tumors. 2) Pre-enucleation radiation for large tumors does not improve survival. 3) Small tumors can often be observed safely until growth is documented.
